newsitem.title: VATICAN: Cardinal denies he backed Argentina's "dirty war".
newsitem.headline: Cardinal denies he backed Argentina's "dirty war".

text.p: A Roman Catholic cardinal on Wednesday denied accusations by a rights group that he had been an accomplice to the Argentine military's "dirty war" on leftists in the late 1970s.

Cardinal Pio Laghi, head of the Vatican's Congregation for Catholic Education, said accusations by the Mothers of Plaza de Mayo that he had turned a blind eye to human rights abuses while Vatican ambassador in Buenos Aires were unfounded.
Laghi, a 75-year-old Italian who is considered a possible successor to Pope John Paul, repeated a denial he has issued several times in the past several years.

"The affirmations of this group of Argentine women are only defamatory and have no content or basis, neither concerning the facts nor on an ethical and legal foundation," Laghi said in a statement issued by the Vatican press office.
He said his activity in Argentina during the period was well documented and available for all to see.

"Recently, I have received from the bishops of Argentina, the heads of the Jewish community...numerous written testimonials of gratitude for what I was able to do in that period to defend...all those who I met who were suffering," he said.

The group's leader, Hebe de Bonafini, repeated the accusations in a news conference on Tuesday. She said she would send a document to Italian Justice Minister Giovanni Maria Flick accusing Laghi of complicity in human rights abuses during the government of General Jorge Rafael Videla.
About 4,000 people died and 10,000 disappeared after the military staged a coup in 1976 and kidnapped anyone remotely suspected of sympathising with the Montonero guerrillas.
The group has several times in the past accused Laghi of knowing about the killings but doing little to stop them.
Bonafini called on Laghi to give up his diplomatic immunity as a citizen of Vatican City and stand trial.
Laghi was Vatican ambassador to Argentina from 1974-1980 during Videla's ruthless military dictatorship.
Videla was convicted of human rights crimes after the return of democracy in 1983 but was freed like all his accomplices by President Carlos Menem's amnesty in 1989.
